text:
I recently got a 4060 to replace an aging 1050 Ti in a rec room ITX cube, specifically the smallest 4060 in existence from ZOTAC since other 4060s are too fat to fit. This mini 4060 is a cute little thing, and for such a small single-fan GPU, both the temps and noise are surprisingly low. Doesn't use much power too, especially compared to the power-hungry RTX 3000 series, and overall, I'm satisfied with it.

That said, a part of me almost wishes I waited for the B580; Intel's basic LE model is about $40 less than a 4060 here in Canada. Not sure if Intel's GPU drivers are reliable enough yet—particularly regarding old games—or if a B580 could even fit in the ITX cube, but it would've been a very tempting option. Regardless, I really hope Intel continues to make GPUs, if only to compete with NVIDIA.

text:
After 6 long years of waiting for a good price-performance card to come out, it seems like it's finally time to switch back to Intel.

When I built my first PC in 2018 and went from gaming at 10fps in 720p on a 2011 ThinkPad T520 with Intel integrated graphics, to gaming at 200fps in 1080p on an RX580 for a mere 180$, it made it hard to justify any subsequent upgrade. I was simply not willing to pay the same amount for an 80% improvement in performance that I once paid for a 3000% one, especially when that improvement wouldn't even allow me to play most modern games in 1080p 60 because of the terrible optimization that seems to be plaguing most titles nowadays.

Perhaps when Intel drops their more top of the line cards, I might consider making the switch.

text:
For all of my long-standing distaste for Intel as a company, and their ongoing disaster of a CPU department, if I were to buy a GPU today it would be this. This is exactly what the PC gaming scene needs - affordable access to good hardware, which we haven't had for half a decade at least at this point. Well done, Intel. I still won't buy your CPUs, but I'll support a GPU underdog delivering good value, and this is clearly that. Now, fingers crossed, we'll see AMD respond to this properly (I'm expecting Nvidia to not compete much on value, though they might improve over current gen), and we might actually have some real competition.

Oh, and the ads in this deserve a call-out for being *hilarious*. Well done, Dennis.

And that VCE "bug" (read: glaring design oversight) is ... wow. Just wow. What the actual f**k, AMD? "Hey, now that we're designing this new encoder block, how about we lock its scaling to a pixel grid that doesn't align with the most common video resolution for the past decade plus?" Seriously, this is just ... no. Just no. Please get it together.

text:
This is an incredible win for budget gaming rigs, for sure, but going by the benchmark results, these cards are a bigger threat to AMD's 17% marketshare than they are to Nvidia's 76%. The fact that the 4060 (Ti) was a bad value was clear from the jump, and these mid-tier Battlemage cards excel in the same sort of tasks that you'd otherwise use an RDNA 3 card for. And yet 4060 variants take up 3 out of the top 10 spots on the Steam Hardware Survey, whereas RDNA-based cards hold... exactly zero spots in the top 10. Clearly, people are choosing the 40 series cards for reasons other than just value (like not wanting to carefully plan your GPU purchase decision around only the use-cases that you have now when you might end up keeping the card for a good 6+ years).

The real question is, if this is what the B580 can do, what would a grown up Battlemage card (B770?) look like in benchmarks?

text:
Intel has really done something here. Let's hope they stick with their strategy. 
One thing i have notices in with this video about GPUs in general: 
Upscaling makes GPU comparisons really hard. GPU A can have better Perfomance but  GPU B  has better upscaling. So if you match them for upscaled image quality (which is also subjective) GPU B perfomes better because the image is more upscaled. Then comes frame generation which can incresy the smoothness wildly but can also introduce input lag and decrease the image quality (which again is subjective). Upscaling introduces an insane amounts of new factors to consider.

text: Please I'm begging you include just one run on Linux, don't test every GPU, just test the single most popular GPU on Linux and put that result on the graph with the rest so we know the difference. Linux gamers are growing with the most recent graph I saw listing 5% of PCs running Linux and 4% running 'Unknown' which almost certainly means also Linux. That's almost 10%! Using Fermi Estimation to adjust for both Steam Decks and an audience that's more likely to use Linux that the average person, I estimate 5% or more of your audience is using Linux - surely that's worth just one bar on the graph? You can even have only one game with a built in benchmark tested with Linux just to list the estimated difference gaming on Linux with an asterisk in the lower right corner of the graph. This video would be especially beneficial since Arc almost certainly doesn't have Linux drivers yet, which is part of the equation. And, just acknowledging Linux like that will have an influence on your audience, and maybe even the industry as a whole.

text: Before AMD was big like it is today, their calling card was always being significantly cheaper than Intel. You saved hundreds on a new build that was not as capable, but could still play the games. I think Intel needs to fill this role for the time being and let its reputation build for GPU and recover for CPU. Regardless of performance claims, these GPU need to always just be the cheapest option. And not just marginally cheaper. They need to be the only sensible option for a budget gaming PC. And, it pretty much is. For now. This can all be undone by Nvidia and AMD with a simple price cut to the 4060ti and 7600xt. I think the only real question is. Can or will they do it. Will they have next gen options around the corner that better compete at the price point? I think red and green would be fools to allow Intel to completely own this price point. I would expect GPU prices to finally come back down to reality, and we will have Intel to thank for it.

text:
Thanks for the review! I do have to agree with others though that the graphs are hard to read (given the short timespan). This doesn't have to be that way! You can tell a lot with well made graphics. Some suggestions:

- Keep the order of the GPUs constant when possible: Instead of sorting by performance, sort them by manufacturer or even better by their category ("equivalent price" and "equivalent approx. performance"). This way we don't have to re-read the whole graph every time and would also make it way easier if you don't know all those random-ass names of those cards by heart. In my case, I can barely remember one number - tell me another and I forget the first one. So a lot of the text (audio and on-screen) could as well be completely random. Icons or images would also help me a lot here.

- While the dots highlighting what you're talking about are nice, they don't actually help me that much, especially when some of the information is on the other side of the screen. You wouldn't highlight sentences in a text just with a dot either, right? Please highlight the whole row!

- The 1%-low bars essentially double the data and thus the mental load/time to parse the screen. Draw them as error bars or just a single small vertical line instead.

- The bar at the top contains a (small) wall of text, i.e. too much to read. Highlight the relevant item (the resolution in this video)! Or even better: Have several icons (1080p, 1440p, 2160p) and highlight the appropriate one. This way it's obvious at a single glance that we're now looking at say the mid-resolution level and you don't need read and parse the text/number "1440p" and go "hmm, okay so that's more than 1080p and what was the third resolution again?"

- Same for the "higher is better". This is supposed to help you understand the graph faster, right? Then why not make it visual too using an arrow: "better =>", again saving a few mental cpu cycles.

- Somebody mentioned color-blindness and while I don't suffer from it I agree that that would be a nice consideration too.

dm me if you want an example graphic. I could even help you implement these ideas :)

text:
A conclusion mentioned early in the video around the 5 minute mark I will dispute. The increased market share of 4K and 1440 displays is NOT due to display price dropping but rather cards able to perform well at those resolutions reaching more mainstream pricing. As the cards performance goes up and prices come down a resolution increase was a natural occurance.

In the display market the more interesting note is not resolution but panel technology. We now see OLED and Mini LED being options are around the $500 and under price point in some cases and notice they are 1440. Mixing newer display tech with better cost for performance the move from 1080 to 1440 is inevitable. Add in things like scaling tech and the move makes even more sense.

So your conclusions that we are seeing this move due to monitor pricing is just wrong.

text:
Growing up I couldn't afford to upgrade to intel parts from saved up pocket money and would buy AMD while thinking Intel does not care about budget gamers so I won't support them when I start earning. Fast forward I saw 7600x price at launch and knowing I didn't need that much processor power bought the 12400F. On GPU side same story for Nvidia and I favored AMD. 
Recently feeling how high my RX580 was drawing power while showing its age, the only good upgrade I could think of was 7700XT. Given how big of a pocket pinch it was I was contemplating to bite the bullet and now B580 has launched . 

Its indeed refreshing and amazing to see intel turn around and be considerate towards budget segment. Hoping they can get their processor edge back to compete against AMD again.

As context I do not upgrade often and try to get the max use out of my hardware before upgrade. My upgrades till date are as follows:

CPU: Intel Pentium 4 -> AMD Phenom ii x4 965 -> AMD FX 6300 -> i5 12400f
GPU: VIA -> Nvidia 9500 GT -> AMD R7 250 -> AMD RX 580 8GB -> (Possibly Intel B580?)
Display resolution: 1024x768 -> 1366x768 -> 1920x1080 (I am not tempted to move to 1440p anytime soon)

text:
I mean, Raytracing is certainly beautiful, but it has always been available - so my essential point is that it has always been a compromise. And choosing to require so much dedicated rt tech I think is pretty lame and obviously a move pushed by nvidia somewhere in the background...... 

Its like people sometimes forget that we have been able to render outright insane graphics for decades if it does not have the constraint of real time. This whole pathtracing/raytracing new naming scheme its such a marketing circus .... ray tracing is just what it is , tracing of rays, and if you make it more complicated it will be more computationally expensive, its pretty simple. And instead of saying "our old implementation was a huge compromise" they come out with a story about how this NEW tech (which is just less constrained) is amazing and brings all kinds of innovation to the table - its so dishonest. While I dont think their RT implementation is bad at all, im trying to show that how you frame it is just a question of perspective..... And its not like physics have not been well aware how to calculate light for over a century almost, its just expensive - and this whole scenario is very descriptive of the job of making game engines/graphics. You always have the "true" formula at hand, but a brute force implementation is impractical.

Calculating light solely as rays is already in itself a simplification of the actual physical phenomena. But within this approach, theoretically there are an infinite amount of reflections, so fundamentally to even start this calculation in the real world, you have to decide when to stop letting the rays reflect anymore, so there is again an inherent compromise no matter what you do. So instead of telling you for example that the reflections gets exponentially less important to the overall calculation for every new layer of reflections , they will emphasize that they added another layer of reflection and its amazing , when really they just wanna make sure your hardware is slightly starved such as to give you the perception that you would gain something with a more potent graphics card. 

I think its very dishonest and something that should be a very illegal practice when you have this amount of control over both the hardware budget and the target for the developers. Because if its not obvious they have almost complete control to create artificial obstacles , such as targeting a computational budget that is not reasonable for anyone besides those who want to sell more ridiculously fast hardware to everyday people.

text: I for one am very excited for intel on this, I have been running an A770 16gb for the last 6 months and it's been an interesting ride particularly because I use linux exclusively. Funnily enough a lot of games that use dx11 or older run significantly better in linux with the arc due to the vulkan translation layers (steam proton and dxvk) shows the full potential of the card, while it's windows performance in the same games are drastically cut down. My best benchmark has been in Overwatch 2, which is a dx11 title that ran around 150 dps on medium to high. But in linux ultra settings I can hold 120, and with fsr easily hold well over 150 fps. That doesn't event begin to mention gamescope and input latency reduction. Overall the a770 makes a fantastic linux gaming card on a budget. And if the B series cards see the improvement we see seeing with the B580 across the generation I am optimistic !

text:
I know when you say things like "this is not a 4k card" you probably mean any game at 4k, including the most unoptimized AAAA titles, but i'd like if you got a little more into detail. I game at 4k most of the time, on my GTX 980 (not ti or super). Obviously not COD, and i cant even open cyberpunk and games using DX12. 

i run mostly high settings on GTA V in 1080p, minus a couple vram expensive settings (using gta v setting's gpu capacity as guide.) Run Dota 2 on mostly high in 4k. I mostly play indie games now though, and they could almost always chug along windowed borderless at 4k at various settings levels.

I obviously would follow your lead and not recommend the GTX 980 for 4k gaming, but i also wouldn't vehemently say this won't do 4k. And you say that about so many cards that are newer than my old 980.

I am looking for a new GPU, hopefully the give my pc some more life, as my GPU is failing and I cant currently afford to do a full replacement at a level my mighty PC once was, but I think i can get away with replacing the gpu to give me DX12 and more GPU power. I have a i7 4790k still, but im very very rarely throttled by cpu, and when i am, its almost purposeful with me abusing my computer with non-gaming programs. 

I had 3x 1080p monitors at the start, but with how much i moved in college, i sold them all and bought 1x 4k monitor. essentially added a monitor and then fused them all.
